div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: A neat Cottage—through the Window, a View of the Harbour.
Mrs. Oakum, and Fanny her Daughter, discovered.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Fanny, my dear—have you been up stairs this morning to the lady?

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: That I have, mother. I went into her chamber before six, but I found her up and dressed—looking from her window out to sea upon the vessels in the offing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: She has won my full confidence, though she reposes none—Notwithstanding she came to us unattended, I am sure she is a person of some condition—and property she clearly has by her liberality. She presented herself here without recommendation—but heaven had written innocence so plainly upon her forehead—I made no enquiries.

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: Father will be home to-day—and, depend upon it, will tell us all about her. How came you never to enquire into her story?

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Because she seemed desirous to conceal it. But, as I imagine you felt no such motive to desist, how happened it that your pretty loquacity never took that direction?

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: O! I have enquired.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Fanny!

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: Yes, indeed!—But silently. I look'd at her eyes, when a storm came on, and saw them cast up to the clouds, full of tears; but they began to brighten, when the sun broke out, and then I was sure she was thinking on her absent lover, and sighing for his safety—I once surprised her gazing upon a picture, and pressing it to her lips—before she could conceal it in her bosom, I saw it was the portrait of an officer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: But why might not this be a husband or a father?

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: O, I'm sure it could not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: And how pray, miss, can you be so clear it could not?

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: Why, la mother, don't I see it must be a lover? Does any body love a husband better than you do, or a father better than I? Captain Oakum has been away from us a twelvemonth—but do we sit as if we grew upon the harbour, and strain our eyes for a month together, to catch even the first peep of his vessel?

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Ah! girl, girl!—These circulating libraries! But, look, Stella is coming down— She seems more than usually pensive—See she passes by our door—Going to the harbour till dinner-time. This is one of her silent days.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Ho, the Oakum yacht! a-hoy!—Man the shrouds there—the commodore is coming on board.

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: Mother, 'tis the voice of Ben Block, I'm sure. Father must be arriv'd.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Bear a-head there you lubber—or fall into my wake—it's all one—only let's get into port—

Ha! Bess, old girl! how fares it, ey—Fan, you jade—why you're as tall as the mizen-mast—Well, old consort, and so the eye-pumps are at work, for joy that Sam Oakum's fast moor'd again. Why you look like the figure of the charming Sally, smiling under our bowsprit yonder—the sun basking upon her forehead, with her cheeks a little dash'd by the spray. Fan! my girl—I've brought you home a ship full of nick-nacks—You'll be set up, I can tell you. There's an Indian canoe, to hang in the hall—a dried alligator, and a tomahawk, with a full suit of Chicasaw armour, all curiously quilted, and arrow-proof.

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: Why, father, what do you mean to make of me?

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Peace, you cuckoo—Let your mother tell me the news in my absence—the house stands, I perceive, just as I left it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: But it has one more inhabitant than you left in it.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: What! hey!—

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Nay, no apprehension—It is a woman, I promise you—and one whom you must be attach'd to, see her when you will. Though you were absent, I did not scruple to receive her into the family—She was an utter stranger, and seem'd unhappy.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Right, my girl—Though the commodore was not on board, humanity is always a standing order of the British navy, and no true seaman ever sheer'd off from the miserable. She's poor, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: No—

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Old and ugly?

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: No—

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Zounds, neither poor, old, or ugly, and yet unhappy—How has she got out of her reckoning, Ben?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Belike, by not allowing for variation and lee-way. Mayhap her consort is on a foreign station—But, if my glass be true, she's just coming into harbour—Speak her, and she'll shew her papers directly.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Good morning to ye all—I rejoice, believe me, in your joy—Captain Oakum, as I have been informed, is arrived—I see himself, I believe, at this moment—Sir, you find here a strange intruder into your family—an object too, commonly of suspicion—a young and unprotected female. The tenderness of Mrs. Oakum has forborne to question me, because she thought her own satisfaction might be my pain—To you I owe such an account of myself, as will I hope prove, that the confidence she placed, without scrutiny, would at least have been justified, if it had been made.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Bless her silver tongue! it's as musical as a first lord of the admiralty's, when he promises a ship to a brave lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: May I beg the favour—
sp.stage: (Making signs to Ben to withdraw Fanny.)

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Save you, my fair snow—I understand your signals. You would have me bear a-head, with the young cock-boat there—Come, miss Fanny, let us obey orders. We'll steer away for the summer-house, and there I'll overhaul my journal to entertain you. I see your inclination is a stark calm—So we'll out with our sweeps, and pull gently off.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: I beg, young lady, you will not think yourself under any necessity of this kind—I desire to know only in what I can render you service.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: I believe it will surprise you to learn that I am a foreigner. I was born in Prussia— My mother was an English woman—at the death of my parents, I resided with a venerable uncle, who is a clergyman. A young baron, whose name is Lindorf, honoured me with attentions—

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Which were not indifferent.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Let me prevent the inference—for it is happiness to own my love for him, and add that he returned it. But our union then was forbidden. Unhappily, for both, a nobleman, high in the prince's favour, thought fit to persecute me with his addresses. Too powerful for slight—too assiduous for evasion, I was constrained to suffer his attentions with an aching heart—At last, with a burning cheek, I speak it—my ear trembled at the avowal of a licentious passion.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: But the young baron—did he know —He did not endure this insult. The profligate—

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Was his uncle. My cries brought the young baron to see him struggling with my resistance—He tore me from his grasp, and left the crest-fallen peer baffled and detected.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: But the result.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: O, sir, you happy English are so accustom'd to be free, you scarcely feel the full blessing of your liberty. What was the result, in states like that! An instant order for my gallant Lindorf to embark for America. Could a soldier refuse the call of his country? Durst he wed in defiance of his sovereign's prohibition? In the presence of the venerable Gellert we solemnly pledged ourselves to each other. Time can never chill affection such as ours.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: You heard from him in his absence?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: For a time I did—Suddenly his letters stopt, and left me only the consolation of his bravery. Of him indeed I could not but hear— Every dispatch to the government dwelt with energy upon his zeal, his courage, and his contempt of danger. We learn'd, at last, that he had been rewarded upon the field with the rank of major.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: The young hero, even in his victories, should have thought of home. When I was at the taking of the San Joseph, I remember writing to thee, old girl, upon the head of the first chest of dollars that was turn'd out.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: It was easier for me to suspect his uncle than himself. Letters might be intercepted —but I deemed his love insensible of change or diminution. A little while since, I learned from the minister's office at Cassel, that he had embarked on his return. Secretly I left my home; at Hamburgh trusted myself to an untried sea, to greet your happy England, where after honourable danger in her service, there could be no bar to his felicity; and my Lindorf might openly take the hand of his fond Stella.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: That period approaches. The transports are arrived with the sick and wounded— Some of the privates must be debark'd at this time.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Let me haste then to gain some intelligence. The humblest of his companions in arms must be interested for him—His bravery, the brightest virtue in a soldier's eye, made him a general mark for observation. Blessed hour! I shall at last then hear one being speak, who has seen my Lindorf.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: There, Mr. Shark—You have made a pretty hand of it. Here are the officers, many of them come back again, and you have had no eye to the main chance.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Why, what would the woman have? Don't I sauce 'em? Don't I make 'em pay? I defy any landlord upon the coast to exceed old Shark in all the mysteries of et cætera.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes, truly—You would take all the merit of making out a bill—though the bar will bear me witness, that every charge flows from my pen, and at least half the items from my imagination.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: You have profited from my instructions, I confess.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Profited from you! As if the daughter of Lawyer Capias needed your help, any help, to make out a bill—Did'nt I act as his clerk for years? The draughts that I have drawn—

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: And do still.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Attending to know counsels' opinion.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: So you do still, in circuit time.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Waiting upon plaintiff, to get instructions for serving process.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Now waiting instructions to serve dinner. The party still demurs to the charges; and commonly orders your bill to be taxed— then sulkily tenders the money at the bar, and so wipes the cause off the paper. But what is this snap I have lost at the military?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What?—listen. When my dear worthy father was in the town—Aye, he had a fine ear.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Only one, you know.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Well, I confess—but the loss of one, I think, strengthened the other—Of a club night, he us'd to turn me his wig off the right ear—

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: He could'nt uncase the wrong one.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: And then did he take in all the little grievances of the tradesmen. In the hurry of the troops to embark, little matters were left unsettled—Some gallant fellow wanted a few necessaries, which exceeded his purse, but not his credit; when they dropt off by the chance of war, the shop-keeper sower'd—curs'd his confidence —then—

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Well, what did old earwig do then?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: What! why he bought up the debts —there was a harvest! A suit upon every one of them—Enter'd back actions upon the dead men, and recover'd fully from their heirs—Why he became himself executor to half the number, and administered to their effects as largest creditor.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: And how did it sit upon his conscience, wife?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Too heavily, I confess—At last he grew qualmish and took to methodism—disinherited me, and built an hospital.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: And this is pious restitution!—Plunder poor fellows who perish for their king and country, to build an hospital with the spoils, and give their grand-children a chance of benefit from the foundation!—Holla! my brace of Sharks —how fare ye, how fare ye?—Here, you see, is honest Ben Block return'd, sound wind and limb—your namesakes have spared me this voyage. But what were your precious heads laid to port about to together?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Shark was complaining of the losses of us trades-people by you gentlemen of the army and the navy.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: O Lord!—O Lord!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: But I told him what my poor father used to say to his clients. Gentlemen, you should return good for evil.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: He had reason—he was a lawyer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: But they did not profit by the doctrine.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Yes, they did. Return good for evil!— why, did they not pay his bill?—But, harkee, a sloop of war has brought in yonder a wounded officer; and who do you think it is? The gallant young Hessian, who came over from Germany with his countrymen, and staid here, until the expedition sailed for America. You remember, he was no bad guest. If you can spare his old quarters, say the word; and I'll make a signal to the vessel.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Mr. Block, do I hear you rightly?— the young Hessian officer?—What, the baron Lindorf?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Aye, aye—Lindorf—the same.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Offer our humble duty to the baron; and assure him, that no guest in the world should keep possession when he requir'd the rooms. All the attention his condition demands shall be paid to him. You have a feeling heart, Mr. Block, will you say all this for us?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Not I—I'd sooner sail to the South-seas. What is the use of so much palaver? If a sailor means you a kindness, he hands you his grog— if you need his assistance, he gives you his purse. If you lose a friend, and take it to heart, he hears your complaint—draws his hand across his eyes— tells you, in a word, that life's a voyage with changeable weather—bids you stick to the needle of Hope, wherever you shape your course, and rely upon the great Steersman of us all.—What else is there in lingo?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Well, then, say it in your own way.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: It shall be done then in two words— All's ready.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE—The Harbour—Soldiers landing at a Distance.

sp.p: Thank Heaven! I am at length at liberty to revisit my family! —The chance of war has left me some few honourable marks of the enemy's kindness. But who is this fair-one seemingly dispos'd to speak to a poor and wounded soldier? When beauty and gaiety fly toward one like me, some absent favourite is usually the real cause, and pity is but the child of love.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Pray, sir, excuse this freedom in a stranger—But you are from America, I think— You seem to have been badly wounded.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Just now landed, madam—the last ration of salt provision here in my knapsack, and not a sixpence in my pocket—maim'd, as you see, and friendless—unknown, and in a foreign land—with hardly any supporters but my courage and my honour.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: You should be a Hessian from your uniform?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: I am, madam. I became this cripple from a musket-ball. We had carried the enemy's outwork: but in the redoubt he was stronger than we expected. Our brave commander was there mortally wounded, and taken prisoner. There too the brave young baron Lindorf was wounded in the face by the push of a bayonet. But for this right arm of mine, which threw up the point of it, he had received it in his body.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Did you preserve him then?—O, let me kiss the hand which sav'd his life!—But say on—inform me, if you can, what else befel my Lindorf?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: For my own part, I was unable to retreat. I fell into the hands of the enemy. The baron made his way good, and follow'd the fortune of the war some time longer. We embark'd on our return the same week. In the last skirmish, he had the misfortune to receive a musket-ball through the right breast.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Madam, take comfort—I have said that he recover'd—we embark'd together.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: O Heav'n, sustain me!— But you say, he lives?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: I have no doubt he does—it was a dangerous wound—but I saw him going on board the sloop of war in the harbour, and he condescended to notice me as he pass'd, saying— “Farewell, my gallant countryman!” and then, laying his hand upon his breast—“Shultzer,” said he, “you see you could not always shield me.”

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Permit me to lead you to my home. Every aid that I can give, or obtain, shall attend your infirmities.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Excuse me, fair lady, but I must refuse you. Every hour's delay is misery to me. Poor and decrepid as I am, thank Heav'n, some faithful beings still long for my return. I shall seek out the commissary—receive what little pay is coming to me—and then seize the earliest opportunity to rejoin my family.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Preserver of my Lindorf!—suffer me, not to reward you—I am too poor—but to present this mark of my gratitude—it will ease, at least, your journey home.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Gracious madam, it is too much— Consider, what did I perform, that any soldier would not have done? The baron was the darling of the corps—he was no officer for parade, vexatious on a field-day, and shy in the field of battle.—I have no worthless pride—but may I return a part?—Compassion may be too kind for the occasion—the tear of pity is apt to blind discernment—Necessity should not be mean enough to take advantage—

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: O keep it, sir—every word you utter, shews how fully you merit it. Let me have the good wishes of so brave a man, and I am overpaid.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Bountiful angel!—

—it is a fortune to me!—In my frugal, virtuous country, this purse bears independence for me! You have bid the soldier close his days in comfort. By your means, I can take my idle chair, in the midst of my children—and, when old age comes on me, chear my neighbours with the recital of the dangers I have escap'd. Then shew the scars of many honourable wounds, and rouze the youthful courage of a brave peasantry.— Heav'n's blessing be upon you, and around you!

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: My dear Stella, I expected to have seen you upon the beach yonder—Mr. Oakum has shewn me there a scene which I can never forget.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: You mean, I suppose, the landing of the troops?—I have had my share of that pleasure, believe me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Impossible!—you should have been upon the very spot—you should have seen the eager eye of the wife, as the boats approach'd, singling out her husband!—the shriek of joy, that announc'd his safe return—the mingled laugh—the hands clasp'd, and rear'd to heaven, in thankfulness—while, from the sea, the distant shout of the soldier, in rough sympathy, replied to it, and bespoke a transport, which none but long-divided friends can ever feel!

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: True, true—but look at the other side of the picture. Did you see that thin and sickly female, whose strength would hardly bear her to the water's edge? With a faltering voice she enquir'd for her husband—she ask'd an old friend, his comrade, more by her eye than her tongue, what had befallen him? The soldier turn'd his eyes upon the ground; and, with a dejected step, silently walked by her. Yes, you who pass your lives in luxury—proud and insensible—get ye to the crouded sea-port— view the poor soldier's return to his native land— mark but the feelings of your fellow-creatures, and become human.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: But see, by the croud yonder, some person of distinction approaches. It is a wounded officer, borne upon a litter.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Support me—my apprehensions are too mighty for my strength.
sp.stage: (Enter Soldiers, bearing Lindorf, who has fainted—Ben Block assisting.)
sp.p: . My Lindorf!—

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: The shock has been too rude—but he seem'd to me rather overpower'd by the fatigues of the voyage, than dangerously ill—his wound evidently requir'd that gentle carriage. Support her, my dear, while I follow them—learn his real state, and the house to which they take him.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: I'll follow thee!—Tell me, do I dream? Where is that ghastly vision which was here, and wore the form of Lindorf? Let me know the worst! Whither have they borne him?—O, these trembling limbs!

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Be compos'd, sweet lady—Mr. Oakum said, 'twas but the fatigue of the voyage —the fear of an unhealed wound—that made them bear him in that way. He is himself gone to learn his state of health, and the house which is to receive him.—See, here he comes.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: 'Tis as I conjectur'd—all will be well. He is received with tenderness at the inn yonder. His wound has been troublesome in the voyage. I have order'd a physician immediately—they will send for an experienced nurse to attend him. But honest Ben Block has volunteer'd his services, and is worth a million—

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Thank you, sir. Excuse me—but I must be the nurse where Lindorf lies. This faithful bosom shall be the pillow for his head— my eye will readiest catch the symptoms of his malady—my hand administer the remedy. A word of hope will console me when he drops to rest, and give me strength to watch him in his slumbers.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Nay, but at least be merciful—I would not for the world, in his weak state—so long absent too—that you should surprise him thus—it might be fatal to him!

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Your pardon! I did not consider.— Right! you must be right—but yet I will be near him. At his chamber-door I may be allowed to sit, without his knowledge. There, every instant, I shall learn tidings of his health. I can, at least, stay any step that presses on too rudely; and silence every noise that might disturb him. Shew me!—shew me, where he is!

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Enter Mrs. Shark and Doctor Cranium.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Walk this way, if you please, doctor.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: Toil of the profession quite insupportable —Genius however can abridge labour. A glance upon the human head suffices to shew all the moral affections of the mind, and all the disorders of the body.—But what is our present subject?

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: A Hessian officer, who was wounded in America, and whose voyage home has much affected—

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: I don't want to know how he is affected —The moment I see the prominences of the cranium, I will tell you how he must be affected.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: But doctor, the baron's wound was in the breast—and therefore pardon me, I don't see how the shape of the head is at all important.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: Shallow!—but thus think all the vulgar. Is not the brain, as it were, the soil in which the nervous tree roots itself? Is not the quantity of brain the measure of all the art, science, wit, valour, patience, fortitude, of the animal man? Yes, madam, there are folded up all the principles of action and the determinations of thought.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Bless me, doctor, it is almost dangerous for a dead man's reputation, to endure the glance of so penetrating an observer.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: Not in the least—I am as secret when I read a scull as the grave, which contained it— I read the dead, that I may serve the living.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: But, Sir, do you never mistake the qualities of these dead subjects?

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: I never hear so—In short I have laid down a map of mankind, by a scale of the encephalon, as easy to be read as a map of the world, but more like that of the moon in its distribution.—But softly—nobody is near us —Mr. Shark is out of hearing; I'll read your character in a moment. Much vital power, irritability and ungovernable desire in that frontal bone. About the root of that nose great compass in the memory of things. Great prominence, I see, in the organ of cunning—That part, if it pressed more boldly upon the forehead, must produce inordinate covetousness, and probably a desire to steal:—as it is, I believe it may content itself with simple overcharge, or common extortion, the usual vice of landladies, and seldom cognizable by law.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Upon my word, doctor—your politeness is excessive.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: So is my discretion—Buried here for ever. Excuse freedom. Science is above forms—besides I could not conceal this from you. But to business—always liberal that way —drop every third fee at the door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You should be agreeable some way. But, as you say—to business. There is here, also, a beautiful young lady—

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: Venus in the train of Mars.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: She will on no account yet venture to see him.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: A mistress!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Sits half the day at the door of the chamber—and begs for quiet below, as though every sound above a whisper were his destruction.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: The very ecstacy of love—fair complexion, light hair, blue eyes, etcætera!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: You will pass her, as you go into his room. He lies in the Mars on the right hand, the first story.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: The Mars I remember. Last patient I had there was a man-milliner from Bond-street —A lady of taste bought him a commission— military pabulum small in quantity—Sickened at the firing of a birthday salute, and died of apprehension. Buried with all the honours of war—happily couldn't hear the vollies over his own coffin!—this however is a patient of another description, and I prepare myself accordingly— subdue pain by the thoughts of glory; and make courage a cataplasm for a gun-shot wound.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: There's one of the age's wonders. This man has frighten'd even philosophers out of their wits. His reading of sculls has made every one of their heads shake upon their shoulders—He does make ludicrous mistakes to be sure sometimes. The other day he lectured upon a nob, which according to him contained immensity of genius; but our sexton, honest Dulman, knew the subject well; the wearer was an idiot from his birth, and performed the office of a cuckow clock in the parish workhouse.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Is this doctor a person of reputation, pray? I hope we may rely upon him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Madam, he is the greatest physician within the bills of mortality—he practises with us here in the season only—and makes excursion and profit together.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Forgive my apprehensions—but you say he may be trusted.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Rely upon it—I hope you think too highly of my sensibility, to imagine I could be indifferent in a case like this—The baron is my old guest—before he embarked for America he resided in this house, and a delightful gentleman he was—

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Gay, and careless I fear!

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Why when he first came among us from his own country, he was a good deal thoughtful, and something melancholy—wrote of a lady called Stella constantly—made verses upon Stella—Stella filled his imagination!

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Well but I hope there was no change —I can hardly speak out my question.
—before he left England,—

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: Yes—before he sail'd, there was some little alteration in him—Gay companions occupied him—but in his wine, he toasted only Stella; and one night, when they brought him from the gaming table, where his losses had been heavy, he only said, “Thank heav'n, my Stella can never know my folly!

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: She sighs to know it now—But pray tell me, these indiscretions must have led him into difficulty.

sp.speaker: Mrs. S.
sp.p: It is a subject of great delicacy, and to be sure there are several debts in the town, which are yet unpaid—I trust no creditor would be so cruel as to force upon him in his present situation.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: O, I beseech you! let us trust nothing to their lenity—I am that Stella you have mentioned —betroth'd to him, and living only in his safety—I have property—I have some ready money, some securities—Instantly let me beg you will seek out these creditors. I will bind myself to satisfy them all—that with returning health no harsh remembrancer of errors past, may cloud the union we have vowed together. Mr. Oakum will, I know, join his security with mine—I will lodge sufficient property in his hands—In a few hours probably we might discover all the claims upon him—oblige me by your haste. At Mr. Oakum's I will meet them—here the noise might be alarming—Such is my love, I tremble till this business is completely settled. Let us instantly about it.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Lindorf on a Couch—Ben Block attending —Dr. Cranium going.

sp.speaker: Cran.
sp.p: Well, well—yes! I know you must be weak—But there is no danger at all—a gunshot wound that endures a voyage from America is never fatal. Besides there is a comforter at hand, who is little dreamt of—but a few hours will explain all this. In the mean time, no agitation! pleasant friends, light food, and good air, will do the business.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Smite me! here's a doctor! Why he prescribes all sunshine and the wind abaft. Whereas an Apothecary's draughts are like a trade-wind, always in your teeth—they lock you up in harbour; and keep you confoundedly sick, though you lie at anchor.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Pray, Mr. Block, will you tell me what acquir'd me so pleasant a friend, and attendant, as yourself?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Ask that of a British seaman! Why you were wounded in the cause of my country in the first place—A foreigner and alone in the second. The reason's plain enough—I thought I could assist you.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: I am indebted to your humanity! It is rarely, I believe, carried to this extent for a stranger.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I'm sorry for it. I like a kindness the better, when it is not a duty. But indeed I have lately found another motive, which I have not told you.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: You excite my curiosity.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Then you must know—Captain Oakum and I this last trip got into port, just before you hove in sight—In the harbour yonder we found, at his moorings, a young lady; a friend of your's!—

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: My expected wife, I conjecture—

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Expected! Ay, may be so—Yes, yes, like enough, I fancy. She is an angel, whom I love to oblige—I could not oblige her more.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: But why have not I seen her? Where is she? I hope she has not suffered by the voyage—Where is she?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Not very far from here.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: What has kept her from me?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Simply fear, that a sudden sight of her might do you more harm than good.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Not in the least—She must be sure at any time her presence would be cordial to me! Pray convey this to her.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: That I will—But she's the only nurse, to whom I would turn my patient over. Yes— she's within soundings, and I'll make you happy in the throwing of a plummet.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: There goes the true sample of the British seaman—He professes nothing, and performs wonders—By his calling almost confined to a churlish melancholy element, he has no taste for compliment, no time for graceful nothings—and his honest bluntness were sometimes in danger to be mistaken, but nature clearly fram'd him so full of heart, the errors of his head pass unregarded.—

— My wife has had a speedy passage indeed! Her caution as to seeing me is rather strange! My wife! aye, my wife! Resentment towards another, and my necessity, made her so—She distinguished me in adversity; I am grateful to her—But O, Stella, the hand you gave away at Cassel, gave with it all my happiness.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: What's this?—A note! From whom?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: The lady: read it.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: “Stella—your own Stella is at hand—In a moment you will see her—Her heart has never strayed an instant from you—this note will prepare you to receive her.”
Stella!—Stella faithful to me—

div.stage: (She runs to him and embraces him—as he recovers she speaks.)

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Let me explain this, my Lindorf— But think not lightly of me, for a step my love has prompted. Perhaps you did write to me— I could imagine they would intercept—Yet was I in some degree consol'd for this, by the proud tribute to your merit, which every dispatch contain'd!

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: O Stella!—

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Nay, more composure, or I leave you. At length I heard that you were wounded, and on your return to England. I instantly determined to come hither and receive you. In this land of freedom, no bar will prevent our union. What property I had convertible is with me; is your's as well as Stella's?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Enchanting excellence!—And you are not then wedded to another?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Another! and you living?—But was there such a report?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Indeed there was. I read it in the letters to the regiment: it was the wound most painful in my breast.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: A mean forgery, to injure me in your esteem.—You did not credit it?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Alas!

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Well, say you did—Truth may be suspected—the evil is not much.—The fullest proof now tells you I am faithful.—I can forgive, though I could never change.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Nay, don't take it to heart; it's only like firing a shot at a vessel you take to be a frenchman; when, suddenly, she hawls down her false colours, runs up the royal standard, and proves to be true british heart of oak. You'll explain best together—I'll cruize in the offing.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: I do not doubt you, Stella—I have endur'd with all a soldier's fortitude—unwholesome situation, scanty food—days of disaster, nights without repose, and last, and worst of all, receiv'd my sword back from an enemy— but these I would have borne, ev'n aggravated borne and blest my fate, to have known, beyond a doubt, that you were mine.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Why dwell thus painfully upon an error, which can have only embittered the past?—Look here, my Lindorf, does this seem like weaken'd love?—See, here is the portrait which you tied about my neck, the evening before you left us—Do you remember our venerable guide, my aged uncle? have you forgotten how, upon the sacred volume, he placed our hands conjoin'd, and call'd on Truth itself, to witness we were one.—That day the father of the village was buried—he had been deeply affected at the loss, and bless'd us with a kind but solemn earnestness.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Rather stab me to the heart than utter it—O fool! rash, unsuspecting Idiot!—The Sun of Heav'n beam'd blessedness upon me: a fiend declared the rays were pestilence, and I must credit the malignant falshood, and rob myself of light and happiness! Since, from this hour, we never more can meet.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: How, never meet?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Too surely never.—O, I have leap'd the precipice, my love.—It is as possible the falling rock should, mocking gravitation, climb the Alps, as I regain the place I once held there.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: What horrid mystery is yet unravelled? —My love, my life, my destin'd husband, speak to me.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Husband—The fiends of persecution call me husband!—With that term, broadly emblazon'd in their flaming hands, they drive me from thee, Stella; and madness is the only friend they leave me!—O Stella, I am lost for ever!

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Madam Stella!—I feel for you from my soul.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Lindorf another's!—has Lindorf a wife?—O what then is Stella?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Could they not spare you one gust?—No; the whole gale of misery beats upon the vessel, and now, behold, she dashes on the breakers.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: O, Victim of inhuman fraud!—Now every thing is clear to me. You have a wife! Dare I contest her rights? they are sacred, and I respect them. Yes, I quit him, and for ever— He will do me justice!—If my distracted brain will give me leave, I will write a farewel blessing to him—then fly as far as these poor wretched feet, or winds and seas will bear me, from the man who never can be mine.

div.head: Scene

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: My dear, I rejoice to see you return'd —you have seen our fair lodger.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: No;—but honest, Ben Block, more unman'd than I ever saw him, told me the story. I hear too, that Stella pledg'd herself to pay the debts which the baron contracted before he embark'd; that the scoundrel landlord Shark, has fish'd up every demand against him, and that the creditors will be here instantly to persecute her.—What has she done since she return'd.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Awhile she sat silent, as if stupified with horror—suddenly she started up, and wrote to the baron—he had been remov'd—the note came back—it contain'd only these few words —“Lindorf, I conjure you write two words from your own hand, to tell me, if it indeed be so, that Stella never can be yours.”—But she has made no enquiry for the answer, and her apartment continues lock'd.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Well Ben, you come here, my honest heart,—

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Like a porpoise before a tempest.— Shark is close behind me, with a glut of dogfish, to worry our poor mermaid. I'll throw a civil bait out to divert their fury; and, if it don't succeed, that ravenous old Shark shall feel my harpoon, I can tell him.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: No, no, Ben, you are too warm.—I will tell them her present unhappy condition; nay, pledge myself to see them fully satisfied, when she is better able to meet them.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: And what do you think will be their answer.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Why, I hope and expect a chearful compliance.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Never belive it;—It's like begging an enemy to spare a ship that has just weather'd a tempest, until she has been into dock to refit.

div.stage: Enter Shark, speaking to some without.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Gentlemen, you had better take a turn or two before the door—I'll open this business for you, and call upon you when it is necessary.

Good morrow, neighbour Oakum—Servant, Madam.—A lady, who is a lodger of yours, sent me to undertake for certain debts in her name, contracted by a Major Lindorf, a friend of hers, before he embark'd on service. If it is agreeable, I should be glad you would acquaint her, that all the creditors are here to wait upon her.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Mr. Shark, it is not necessary I should remind you of what passed this morning under your own roof.—A young lady, like Stella, disappointed in her dearest hopes, is, as you may think, struck down by the calamity. She is in no state for business: besides, the baron is here himself to answer for his own engagements.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Why, as to her condition, to hear of a wife at the very minute when she would have elop'd with the husband, was rather unlucky; but for the baron's answering his own engagements, he is in no condition to think about them; and, besides, he has left my house.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Well, but a little time humanity might grant, neighbour—even were your notion of her character a just one.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: It's as false as a fire-ship.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Why, lookee! you must not suppose, Captain Oakum, that I'm a child in business at these years!

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Nay, but a day or so.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Not an hour.—Why may not she set off from Bristol as well as the Major?—A townsman like you, Captain Oakum, should have more feeling for your neighbours.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Sir, if my duty as a townsman call upon me to violate my feeling as a man, I shall change my habitation and preserve my character.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Gentlemen, I find it will be necessary you should assert your just rights here: pray walk in.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: So, here they come!—What a yell you are making there about your demands and your losses. How you clamour now for instant payment, when, yesterday, you would have taken sixpence in the pound, and blessed yourselves. And you, old Shark, would most probably have brought 'em up at that rate, for you know your crooked rib fired a volley of curses at you for neglecting it.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: A libel! a libel!—My wife is a woman of the nicest principle.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: How the devil did she come by it? Is she not the daughter of old Capias? And don't I know a pettifogging lawyer always buys a bad debt as a jew does a bad shilling?

div.stage: (Stella enters with a countenance of forc'd composure.)

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Nay, cease this outrage! I am come to satisfy you!—

—Your kindness led you to ask for me a few short hours of rest, which the cruelty of these men denied me; but, while I remember any thing, your tender offices in my behalf shall never from my mind.—For him, the object of every hope, and almost every thought, my Lindorf, this, my last act, shall prove my love; for all that I possess I give to his necessities.—

— Here are bills, into which I converted the little I could call my own; I brought them over to aid me in my views of happiness—those prospects, blotted out for ever, what can I hope from trash like this?—She, who is struck to the very soul as I am, can never feel the comforts which these may purchase.—Take them— pay yourselves—but leave me.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Come, gentlemen, you had better retire, I think now, to the King's Head. As here seems property sufficient to pay your demands, we need not intrude upon the lady, while we settle the proportions.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: No, truly, kind considerate creditors: and I shall beg leave, on the part of this lady, to assist at the settlement, lest your scrupulous consciences take advantage, and pay yourselves twice over.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: Come, gentlemen, to the King's Head.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Harkee, old offender! Arn't you asham'd to set up such a sign as that? the King's Head! Why, it is always as a beacon, to guide the unfortunate into harbour; and what must that scoundrel merit, who uses it before the den of extortion?—D'ye hear!— Would you have a true sign of what the house contains, hang up yourself, and recommend your wife within doors—the halves exactly tally—that will be honesty.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: —Here are the precious pledges of his faith—dear sacred bonds, all cancelled now—come to my heart.—O, why should I look at lines that will be the last effac'd from my poor brain?— What's this which shoots from my heart's centre upwards?—It burns the very artery it flies through!—Hark! some one comes!—'Tis she! your wife!—Lindorf, detain me not.—Think you I would not beg, starve, die, rather than mar your comfort?—Away! pursue me not!— What would you have more?—Look, I have heal'd the wounds of your imprudence—every thing is paid—and now, light as the winds, I rush upon my course; and quitting man, and all his perjuries, fly to the howling desart for protection.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Well, thanks to my precaution, Old Shark has been a little narrowed in his prey. Had I left him to settle with the knaves undisturbed, the balance would have sunk out of notice in a twinkling.—I hope Stella is more compos'd.

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: The sweet creature!—alas!—she's gone—positively gone from us! When she broke away in that agony produc'd by those creditors, I concluded she had rush'd into her chamber, and sought for consolation in solitude—but I mistook; her emotions were the low workings of despair—louder complaint was for much lighter sorrow.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: She cannot have left the town—

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Why, so I thought—and our worthy Ben Block went hastily in search of her. He came back in a fit of melancholy—said she had been seen hurrying along the road, and at length running as if pursued. You know his sullen kind of tenderness—After a few low-mutter'd curses, half-choak'd by sobs, and his usual vociferation against all the rascalities of the lubbers ashore, he told me he was underway—a voyage of discovery—mayhap he might cast up again, mayhap not—but he would seek the poor wretched wreck, that had neither rudder or compass, and either pilot her into port, or perish in her company. Is it not strange he should attach himself to an entire stranger, whose habits and excellences are so much above him?

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Are so much above him!—A British sailor never stays to ask the rank of the unhappy —shew him but misery, he springs to its relief—humanity with him is no affair of prejudice or calculation. I have seen honest Ben at one minute tear up his cravat to bind the wounds of a messmate; and the next plunge into the sea; to rescue a drowning enemy. Such is the English tar—Do you wonder we are lords of the ocean?

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: O my dear father!—there is an old gentleman, just arrived, who enquires after the foreign lady. He begs to see you, or my mother.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: The uncle, rely upon it, whom she left so rashly! What shall we say to him, in our present alarm and uncertainty?

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: That must depend upon the temper of his mind. Yet, in any case, can we deceive him? She, whom he thinks to meet, is absent— the darling, whom his hopes presage here, and in health and beauty, stung to the soul, is hurrying o'er the waste, a fugitive, frantic and houseless.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Hush!—he's here.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Sir, madam!—Distress, like mine, may violate the laws of ceremony, and the offence be venial.—I am come from the north of Germany —from Cassel, old as I am, alone, to seek my age's comfort. O! the weary search that I have made! But here, I trust, my long, long chace will end!—At my landing, I was told that a young lady, such as my Stella, arrived—not many weeks are pass'd—from Hamburgh. You, I learn, receiv'd her. Stella—Stella Gellert was her name. If I am right, content me in a word, and make an old and weary traveller grateful.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Sir, they told you truth. Stella did arrive at this port, and, by my wife here, was received into my family.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: She is still with you, sir?

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: At the present moment, she is absent—

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: Merely, sir, from home just now.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: O, do not trifle with me!—She little needs deny herself to me. I bring no persecution —no upbraiding! Old as I was, my house had sanctity enough to shield her from the oppressor. She chose to quit it—without a word to leave me—that was unkind enough to her fond second parent. She will not, when I have cross'd the sea, to look upon her ere I die—O, she will not drive me away, like an unwelcome guest, and thus disown me in a foreign land!

sp.speaker: Mrs. O.
sp.p: There is no unkindness in her mind. We are acquainted with her story—know your interest in her happiness. We have heard too of her unworthy persecutor.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Indeed he was unworthy—but as the hour of repentance did arrive to him, let us, in charity, hope it was effectual. Yet he carried his resentment to a mean extent. Not content with having driven the young baron across the Atlantic—to give him torture exquisite indeed, he forwarded unquestioned proof, that his fond Stella had been married to another.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: What a pity it is that a villainous design should ever be successful!

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: How successful? Know you any thing of the baron Lindorf? Is he arriv'd in England? I heard he had been wounded; and it was no small inducement to my journey, that here I hoped to find my wanderers; and that myself, at last, might witness vows which no earthly power could annul.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: He is return'd—and they have met.— Enough at this late hour! Age and anxiety demand repose. To-morrow you will know every thing.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: But shall I see my Stella in the morning?

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: As certainly, as I hope myself to see her.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Friends, I rely upon you. Thanks for this promis'd comfort. For the night, then, I must rest satisfied. To-morrow will give her to my arms. Till then fatigue will prove an opiate strong enough, to make the hours insensibly drag on. Fancy may even anticipate the morrow —and bless the mental sight with its first joy, Stella! arrayed in innocence and duty.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE—A Field—in Front, an open Shed to house Cattle, with a Hay-loft above it— upon some Straw on one Side, hardly visible, Stella sleeping.

sp.p: Zo—zo!—never at rest, I think. Our Zue came running whoam last night, just at dimmet, blaking and creunting as if she had zeen a ghoast.—Noathing will zatisfy her, but that zome vine thing, all in white, ran under our tallet yonder. I'm as much a mon as anither, an if they be for chounting me; but if they gally me with faeries and zuch, there be but a very thin speuring indeed between me and a coward.—Theck pleace be a dom'd unlucky one, zure enough. I'll call vurst—If there be ony zivil christen there, why he'll give one a zivil answer. —Whoa! holla! be ony body in theck tallet? —Noa—noa! Zue's gone hantick, a' think.— I'll venture—

— Mercy on's!—here be zome one, zure enough! —all cover'd o'er with the briss and dirt of the road!—A leady, vast azleep upon the straw!— her be main handsome!—Zoft! she do stir.— I'll step azide a bit—we shall zee azoon what madam would be at.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.stage: (rises, comes forward, and then sits on a rude seat in front)
sp.p: —No fear of persecution! —Here I can sit and view the wintry storm strike down the lingering foliage, and ere long the genial spring replenish all again—but on my breast, all chearless, blank, and blighted, no beam of happiness will ever fall. Here I can sit, and study yon pure heaven, until my senses, light and unconfin'd, escape this groveling clod, and soar to peace.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: A zee that she be no stranger—she do call me by my name at first sight.—Here I am, at your zervice, madam—honest Jacob Clod, of Shepton-mallet.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: What would you?—Pray, leave me! A shelter, such as this, may be allow'd me!— Cold wind and rain should not be envied me! The villainy of mankind has driven me from society —O do not vex my solitude!

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: I desdain to vex any body, I.—Poor zoul! she be main unprovided to run from habitation. —I suppose there will be no offense in bringing her a bit, to stay her stomack—though she be too apurt and proud to accept an invitation to dinner.—
—Madam, theck tallet of mine be but a damp, coad sort of a bedchamber. I'ave a cottage hard by, wi' a good warm thatch to cover 'en; and there be always a corner in my chimney for the unhappy.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: No!—Do not molest me!—I cannot accept your offer. Like the birds, innocent tenants of your fields, suffer me to pluck my scanty food, and wander where I will. Were I not friendless, pennyless, I would reward you!

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: Reward!—I despise it!—I'ave a small farm, well stockt—my children dutiful, and not one bad crop in five. I am a poor unletter'd mon; but this I know, the best return that we can make for quiet nights, and days of prosperous labour, is never to add a bolt to our door, for fear Misfortune should lift up the latch to enter.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Well, I will not dispute this with you. You may be honest—however others have dealt with me! Try not, I implore you, to win me from this hovel—I will not quit it—while I must linger in this bad world, it is my home. Your charity (I see you are not devoid of it) may fence me from the night-dews; and you have children, whose innocent hands may bring plain simple diet, bread and milk, to feed me. Promise me this, and leave me!

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: Well, well—in the hope, that ere long you may take better mind to ye, and in a happier mood accept more kindness from me, I'll promise. I'a learnt, at least, one thing in this life—to allow a vriend to be happy in his own way. And though your comfort, I fear, be but slender, I'll not make it less by teazing you into more accommodation than suits your fancy.—
sp.stage: (Stella sits down in a contemplative posture.)
sp.p: — Poor zoul! she have a marvellous liking for my tallet—and is like to be sole inhabitant, unless our kees dispute it wi' her in a thunder-storm. I mun send Zue to un wi' some milk, and zoforth —and then to tawn, to look in upon cryer— ten to one, some poor christen zoul be breaking's heart about her. It's a good deed I go about, and one day's threshing at the barn will not be missed in a season.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: The harpies thought to seize my Lindorf—he had fought, and bled too—was dying for their country—but what of that?—What's country to the cruel creditor? —Thank Heaven! I had means to save him then—they were all I had—I gave them for him, who dearly loved me once—now I am nothing —want nothing.

div.stage: Enter Shultzer, not at first seeing her.

sp.speaker: Shark.
sp.p: By this hay-loft, I should be near some farm.—Here's one who will instruct me. Lady, will you have the goodness to teach a wounded soldier where he may obtain some refreshment on his march?—Sure I have seen that form—my benefactress—my bounteous mistress —O tell me, what means this change—why do I find you here—why thus? Do you forget the being you made joyful?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Not I—One being I design'd to make supremely blest—years did I meditate his happiness —that string for ever with its silver note made up hope's harmony. But then, friend, an iron hand struck the frail trembling fibre, so fiercely struck it, the poor chord was snapt, and all is discord now.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: O miserable world!—thrice wretched man!—a little while since I left thee, fair-one, and thy bounty chear'd me with thoughts of home and independence! I find thee now smitten, in distraction—a rude hovel all thy shelter, and no friend nigh to soothe thy malady. I cannot bear it—my old rugged cheek, which dar'd the fate of war, is now moist as my mother's, when I first swore that I would be a soldier, and her weak fancy saw me instant shot, and dying in the battle.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Soft you—a word with you—I know you now—that look—that dress—you once preserv'd him too—you are a soldier, sir, a veteran. At Cassel, an old viper crawls, who stung a friendless innocent! Do not you venge my wrongs— I'm going thither straight—my brain will bear the memory of 'em.—I will but shew him his full triumph! Sob out my injuries and my despair; and perish at his feet!

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Why this is enough to make one lothe life altogether!—The faithful, the affectionate, the gentle, the humane, levelled in a moment with the vilest in condition, and the weakest in understanding! What is best to do?—She must have friends in Bristol—I'll back thither to find them. Great as is my longing to greet my wife and children, charity, as well as gratitude, compels me to delay the satisfaction!

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Save ye! save ye, brother!—Are you one of the natives, or only upon a cruize in these latitudes?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: A fellow-traveller.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I see you have suffered in your profession, —I always thought that war was the best school of humanity. I have a freight of grief here that threatens to start my timbers.—Will you help me to bear it?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Soldier and sailor, as they are partners in glory, should share the rubs of the world with equal readiness.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Then mark me. The case, d'ye see, is this—A young lady yonder has lighted on a hurricane, where she expected a calm—Cross'd in love, by the bearing down of a yankee consort, she has unshipped the rudder of her right wits, and drives at large here with neither chart nor compass—Will you aid me in the chace of her?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: You do not wear the dress of a persecutor, and I may look upon you as the steady friend of innocence. Our search is needless— She is found.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Your hand to that, brave boy.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: There it is—The lady you seek is the friend of baron Lindorf—her name Stella de Gellert—she is here.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Ay! but in what state, eh!—under whose care?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: That rude tenement at present holds her—nor do I think another being knows her situation and necessity. I have seen and spoken with her.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Well and eh! How did she answer ye? must she be condemn'd, or can the doctor set her to rights, and make her answer the helm again?—Why, d---mme, how I snivel!—

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: What she said rather sounded like the result of sudden anguish, and hurried fancy, than fix'd and rooted madness,—But some one comes this way.

div.stage: Enter Susan, with a Jug of Milk and a small Basket of Bread, &c.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Come hither, sweetheart—Tell me where you live, and where you are going to?

sp.speaker: Susan.
sp.p: I am only going into our tallet yonder. Feather have sent me with some refreshment to a poor lady beside herself, that have run in there for shelter—I don't think she will harm me.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I'll warrant ye not—you live—

sp.speaker: Susan.
sp.p: There yonder—that be our own smoke coming out of theck chimney.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Hold, here's a ribband for thee at fair-time. —Will you promise to see the poor lady then as often as you can—and as long as she will suffer you?

sp.speaker: Sus.
sp.p: That I will, kind sir!—I shall be back soon at home, if you please to look in there.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: What's your design in desiring the child's attendance on her?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I'll tell you. When I have been sour'd myself in the world—Come home from a voyage worse than I went out, my prizes retaken, and no insurance made upon 'em by the lazy lubber of a husband ashore—I've been for staving in the bulk heads, and sousing to the bottom in despair:—But, while in this trim, some good spirit or other has flung, as it were, by chance, a little child in my way; and what happened then? First, my legs parted company to admit the prattler into harbour—My fingers next, somehow or other, got entangled in the hair of the elf—in a second, it was on my knee; and its inquisitive eyes asking why I was dumb-founded? I do'nt know how it was—but, sooner or later, my wind-pipe began to swell; the sorrow I had shipt ran plentifully out of my scuppers—I kiss'd my little doctor in transport, and then fairly turn'd myself to make the best of a bad adventure.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: Nature always speaks the language of wisdom I have children myself, who will console me for all I have suffered.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Have you children, soldier? I take that to be a true charter party in a voyage of benevolence. Let us first to the cottage—We can then shape our course, and seek out friends and assistance. You shall soon bring the doctor's chest to bear down this way; and my old commander and his consort will join us directly. Trust me, brother, he who makes a little leeway to do a kind action, when he hands up his log-book above, will not be found much out in his reckoning!

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: You are sure then that this person answers our description?

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: Zure! Lord aye, for zertain—but I don't ask ye too much, when I only beg you to zee un, and zatisfy yourselves.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: And I would instantly go thither—did I not fear the sight of her old uncle might add another pang to those she suffers; and these feeble limbs seem to reproach her for having fled me, without a line, in pity left, to hint the cause or object of her flight.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Therefore, Sir, you shall for the present remain here, until we have ascertain'd how she is able to bear your interview.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Save you, noble commander—All hands here to clear the wreck?—But I have just parted with a brave fellow, who has shot away like a rifle ball for the doctor—He has seen madam Stella, and calls her his benefactress.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Did you ask his name, Ben?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Not I—What does it signify?—I wanted assistance, and he answer'd the call— said he knew Lindorf, and her connexions— When a wounded soldier, anxious to join his family, stops in his course to lend a tow-line to us in our trouble, curiosity would look like suspicion, and strikes honest humanity, like a shot from a cruizer, to bring the vessel to.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: You have not yet ventur'd yourself into Stella's sight?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Why, no—All is in train for that—A young cherub is in her wake just now, whose innocence may reconcile her, in some degree, to lubbers like us. She'll stand several points nearer to the wind, than a hulk like me.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.p: My daughter Zue, be liker a cherub than her mother for zertain—She will be main delighted to be useful—and I shall be proud and happy in my child—But pray ye gentlevolks walk into my cottage, and command every thing in my possession.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Readily friend—We are all of us at times disposed to doubt whether virtue have not left this world entirely. But if she should be frighten'd from our crouded and dissipated cities, while the British farmer preserves his plain and simple manners, there is no fear, I think, that the nymph will ever desdain the shelter of his humble thatch.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.—A Field with the inside of a Shed.
Stella sitting with little Susan endeavouring to divert her.

sp.speaker: Sus.
sp.p: There, madam—I'm sure you be handsomer for these flowers—Will you let me be your maid, and take me along with you to your fine house?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: I must attend, I find, in spite of me. Alas! my home is in a foreign country—You would not leave your father, Susan?

sp.speaker: Sus.
sp.p: I could return to see him at harvest time.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Why then, my dear?

sp.speaker: Sus.
sp.p: O then, I'm a little queen, you know —all over ribbands and cranks and things—You would not know me—but you will let me prepare a room, for you at the farm? Bless you, madam, say yes now—and send me joyful home to father?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Even as you will, sweet one—You are a queen, and must be obeyed in all things.

—The tumult of my mind subsides —Great Power! I thank thee, that my poor brain recovers from the shock; that I have strength to measure and to bear my strong afflictions! Lindorf has a wife!—Learn to endure that, Stella, and the rest is but the wasp to one already bitten by the adder. When this warm bosom has repress'd its fires, and age has temper'd all—some offspring of my Lindorf may be taught to look upon me as another parent, and love my memory when he shall lose me.

sp.speaker: Gellert
sp.p: I will not be withheld—Who should console his suffering child but Gellert?—Let me speak peace to her and mild forgiveness.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: My dear, my reverend uncle—Oh! holy man, forgive a fond, weak girl, who, flying your protection, lost herself. But could you know the anguish of this breast—wild and ungrateful as is my conduct—you would think it expiated.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Dear sufferer, I do not reprove thee— My calling which leads me to observe at full the weaknesses of others, has not, I trust, concealed from me my own. Our common imperfection should render us all placable to repentance.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Thus, after a day of storm and agitation, the evening comes in grey and serene at last, though somewhat clouded—But I shall not, I hope, lose my fair friend?

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: No, Sir.—I have resolved to close my days with her in England—Here, time, and my fond cares may at length succeed, and the future years bring to my Stella healing on their wings.

div.stage: He passes hastily up to Stella, and kneels.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: My heart is full, fair one—The faces of all here tell me it may overflow without danger. I will kiss your fair hand if you please now —I must soon ask permission of another. I have not been idle, and I was always bad at telling a long story. There's a soldier without, who has a right to the honest gratification of conferring happiness for happiness received. May I introduce him?

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Ben—why you are upon the main-top to-day.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: The top-gallant mast head—and the colours I carry are true blue.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: What does this mean, my child?

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: I think I guess, Sir. I was so fortunate as to meet a veteran soldier—he was of Hesse Cassel—wounded and distress'd. He had serv'd under (no matter whom) had serv'd him also—sav'd him. He comes to tell me, that my casual bounty has been the source of some good fortune to him.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: There brother—I have only thrown the lead for you, to ascertain the soundings—you're now abreast of the fort—may fire the salute yourself, and deliver your dispatches.

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: First, madam, allow your grateful servant to rejoice in the change a few short hours have produced. It would have embittered your bounty, to have reflected upon calamity such as I witness'd. But I am come to give you joy indeed—Lindorf, your adorer, and my gallant commander, is still your own.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: I mean, at liberty to be so. The health of the countess, his late wife, was much impair'd when she embark'd for Europe; but too impatient to undertake the voyage and meet her husband, on the passage she fell a sacrifice to the rashness of her attempt.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: Sir, you are too good a man, to state this upon slight grounds. But, I have learn'd by frequent failures in this fickle world, not to yield too ready an assent. How did these tiding reach you?

sp.speaker: Shultz.
sp.p: The messenger is without, and will instantly attend you.

div.stage: Lindorf enters, and clasps Stella to his breast.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Yes, my ever destin'd wife! I may now indulge the hope of happiness! She, who is no more, demands my gratitude! She distinguished me in my ill fortune, and enabled me by her partiality, to do full justice to my Stella.

sp.speaker: Stella.
sp.p: Oh, Lindorf! various emotions crowd in upon my soul! Do not imagine me insensible of the blessing I have so ardently desir'd— But this is a solemn moment—and I am to receive your vows in the presence perhaps of one, who lov'd you equally, but to whom the Great Disposer of affections denied a life devoted to your happiness.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Never were you dearer to me than at this moment. In our happiest hours, endear'd by mutual affection, and adorn'd by affluence, we will together bend with gratitude to our liberal benefactress.

sp.speaker: Gell.
sp.p: And this is the frame of mind best suited to our welfare—Our joy temper'd by such respect for a departed friend, is fitted to our natures; in which unmix'd extremes of either delight or sorrow are apt to wound alike.

sp.speaker: Oak.
sp.p: Joy sparkles in every eye, and every tongue is impatient to congratulate.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: In that case, manners might keep me too long a-stern. I therefore run a-head with my salute. Long life to you, my hearts—may you always answer the helm (to Stella) and you always keep a true reckoning (to Lindorf) so will your voyage be steady and prosperous, and may the gale of a good Providence always blow right aft, till you reach the common harbour of us all.
